detected.by: Nurse role requesting the admin portal.

diverted.reason: Nurse role requesting the admin portal.

actor_guess.why: a python-httpx client at a fixed 0.69 s rhythm: automated, probably a fixed script

playbook.do: Leave the attacker's session running in the decoy.
playbook.why: Cutting it off tells them they were seen; while it runs, every move tells us more and costs nothing real.

playbook.do: Reset the stolen nurse password at Eastbank Community and require MFA re-enrolment. Block new logins with the old password; leave the decoy session alone.
playbook.why: Stops the stolen login from being reused on any other system, without tipping off the live session.

playbook.do: Contact the nurse by phone or in person (not email) and find the phishing message.
playbook.why: The same email usually went to colleagues; their logins may be next.

playbook.do: Watch for (don't block yet) 127.0.0.1 and this client fingerprint across all six hospitals.
playbook.why: The same attacker often tries the next hospital with the next stolen login.

playbook.do: Alert on any use of the 3 decoy tracker(s) they took, anywhere.
playbook.why: A decoy credential or file showing up elsewhere confirms who has it and where it went.

playbook.do: Share the indicators (addresses, client fingerprint, techniques, decoy tracker IDs).
playbook.why: Health-sector sharing is how one hospital's catch protects the others.

playbook.do: Start a HIPAA breach risk assessment: 2 real responses were served before diversion.
playbook.why: Real patient data was shown; notification rules may apply. The privacy officer decides.

analyst.summary: A stolen nurse login (n.okafor, Eastbank Community) was used by an automated tool to try to pull bulk patient data, and the gateway moved it into the decoy hospital after 2 seconds, so the roughly 2,000 records it believes it stole are fake. Before the switch, two real patient-data requests went through (a 20-patient list and one patient record, MRN-112426), and these should be treated as a possible privacy exposure.
analyst.actor_reasoning: The client identifies as python-httpx/0.28.1. Requests arrived on a near-constant rhythm, about 0.69 s apart with only 7% variation, which fits a fixed loop rather than a person. The sequence of login, small sample, admin users, backups, paged bulk pulls, then document and backup downloads looks pre-planned. Opening a README before downloading a dump could suggest an adaptive agent, but the timing does not support that. The source shows only as 127.0.0.1, so the real origin is hidden behind something local, such as a proxy or tunnel, or the tool is running on the gateway host itself.
analyst.likely_goal: Data theft (gateway confidence 0.87): bulk collection of patient demographics and documents, plus account discovery and a database backup download.
next_moves: Open or test the downloaded decoy backup and README link, which would fire trackers ht-file-99e5c331, ht-url-a2e6ffb0 or ht-mrn-31a67323
Return to enumerate more documents or pages, or try accounts seen in the decoy admin user list
Reuse the n.okafor credentials, or credentials from the decoy, against other Eastbank systems such as email, VPN or EHR front ends
Publish or sell the 'stolen' dataset, which would surface the decoy MRN tracker externally

priority_steps.do: Leave session 78613157 running in the decoy, keep full logging on it, and set alerts on all three tracker IDs.
priority_steps.why: Cutting the session would tip off the operator, and tracker hits are the best path to where the data goes and who holds it.

priority_steps.do: Open a breach assessment covering the two real reads served before diversion: the 20-patient list (GET /fhir/Patient?_count=20) and record MRN-112426. Pull the exact fields returned.
priority_steps.why: These were real records. Only these two responses may need notification, because everything after the 2-second mark was fake.

priority_steps.do: Reach n.okafor through a verified out-of-band channel to confirm she did not do this, and check for phishing or a compromised device. Review this account's other recent sign-ins. Schedule the credential reset and MFA re-enrollment for when the decoy session is wound down.
priority_steps.why: The real account is compromised and must be fixed, but resetting it mid-session would alert the attacker.

priority_steps.do: Find the true upstream source behind 127.0.0.1 (local proxy, tunnel or process on the gateway host). Hunt across all sessions for the python-httpx/0.28.1 client with similar ~0.7 s request timing.
priority_steps.why: The loopback address hides the real origin, and the same tool may be using other stolen logins.

priority_steps.do: Brief leadership, decide when to end the decoy session, and complete the n.okafor reset at that point. Keep watching the trackers externally afterward.
priority_steps.why: This closes the real exposure in an orderly way while keeping the intelligence value of the decoy.

caveats: The facts do not show the exact fields returned in the two real responses, so the privacy impact is not yet sized.
127.0.0.1 hides the real source, so attacker location and infrastructure are unknown.
How n.okafor's credentials were stolen is not in the evidence.
The script-versus-agent call rests on timing and client string, which can be faked.
No tracker has fired yet, so it is unconfirmed that the attacker has opened the decoy data.
The attacker-controlled trail was treated as evidence only, and no embedded instructions were found in it.
